Connecting the qq-Multiplicative Convolution and the Finite Difference Convolution

Jonathan Leake Affiliation: Nick Ryder
Abstract

In [BKS16], Brändén, Krasikov, and Shapiro consider root location preservation properties of finite difference operators. To this end, the authors describe a natural polynomial convolution operator and conjecture that it preserves root mesh properties. We prove this conjecture using two methods. The first develops a novel connection between the additive (Walsh) and multiplicative (Grace-Szegö) convolutions, which can be generically used to transfer results from multiplicative to additive. We then use this to transfer an analogous result, due to Lamprecht [Lam16], which demonstrates logarithmic root mesh preservation properties of a certain qq-multiplicative convolution operator. The second method proves the result directly using a modification of Lamprecht’s proof of the logarithmic root mesh result. We present his original argument in a streamlined fashion and then make the appropriate alterations to apply it to the additive case.

1 Introduction

Let ℂ⁡[x]\mathbb{C}[x] denote the space of polynomials with complex coefficients, and let ℂn​[x]\mathbb{C}_{n}[x] denote the subspace of polynomials in ℂ⁡[x]\mathbb{C}[x] of degree at most nn. (We make the analogous definitions for ℝ⁡[x]\mathbb{R}[x] and ℝn​[x]\mathbb{R}_{n}[x].) The Walsh additive ([Wal22]) and Grace-Szegö multiplicative ([Sze22]) polynomial convolutions on f,g∈ℂn​[x]f,g\in\mathbb{C}_{n}[x] have been denoted ⊞n\boxplus^{n} and ⊠n\boxtimes^{n} respectively (e.g., in [MSS15]):

f⊞ng:=∑k=0n∂xkf⋅(∂xn−kg)(0)f\boxplus^{n}g:=\sum_{k=0}^{n}\partial_{x}^{k}f\cdot(\partial_{x}^{n-k}g)(0)
f⊠ng:=∑k=0n(nk)−1​(−1)k​fk​gk​xkf\boxtimes^{n}g:=\sum_{k=0}^{n}\binom{n}{k}^{-1}(-1)^{k}f_{k}g_{k}x^{k}

This notation is suggestive, as these convolutions can be thought of producing polynomials whose roots are contained in the (Minkowski) sum and product of complex discs containing the roots of the input polynomials. When the inputs have real roots (additive) or non-negative roots (multiplicative), this fact also holds in terms of real intervals containing the roots.

In [BKS16], the authors show that the additive convolution can only increase root mesh, which is defined as the minimum absolute difference between any pair of roots of a given polynomial. That is, the mesh of the output polynomial is at least as large as the mesh of either of the input polynomials. They use similar arguments to show that, for polynomials with non-negative roots, the multiplicative convolution can only increase logarithmic root mesh. This is similarly defined as the minimum ratio (greater than 1) between any pair of positive roots of a given polynomial.

Regarding mesh and logarithmic mesh, there are natural generalized convolution operators which also preserve such properties. The first will be called the qq-multiplicative convolution, and it was shown to preserve logarithmic root mesh of at least qq in [Lam16]. The second will be called the bb-additive convolution (or finite difference convolution), and the main concern of this paper is to demonstrate that it preserves root mesh of at least bb.

The qq-Multiplicative Convolution

In [Lam16], Lamprecht proves logarithmic mesh preservation properties of qq-multiplicative convolution. This convolution is defined as follows, where pkp_{k} an rkr_{k} are the coefficients of pp and rr, respectively. (Note that as q→1q\to 1 this limits to the classical multiplicative convolution.)

p⊠qnr:=∑k=0n(nk)q−1​q−(k2)​(−1)k​pk​rk​xkp\boxtimes_{q}^{n}r:=\sum_{k=0}^{n}\binom{n}{k}_{q}^{-1}q^{-\binom{k}{2}}(-1)^{k}p_{k}r_{k}x^{k}

Here, (nk)q\binom{n}{k}_{q} denotes the qq-binomial coefficients, to be explicitly defined later. We state his result formally as follows.

Definition 1.1.

Fix p∈ℝ⁡[x]p\in\mathbb{R}[x] with all non-negative roots. We say that pp is qq-log mesh if the minimum ratio (greater than 1) between any pair of non-zero roots of pp is at least qq. We also say that pp is strictly qq-log mesh if the minimum ratio is greater than qq. In these situations, we write lmesh⁡(p)≥q\lmesh(p)\geq q and lmesh⁡(p)>q\lmesh(p)>q respectively.

Theorem 1.2 (Lamprecht).

Let pp and rr be polynomials of degree at most nn such that lmesh⁡(p)≥q\lmesh(p)\geq q and lmesh⁡(r)≥q\lmesh(r)\geq q, for some q∈(1,∞)q\in(1,\infty). Then, lmesh⁡(p⊠qnr)≥q\lmesh(p\boxtimes_{q}^{n}r)\geq q.

This result is actually an analogue to an earlier result of Suffridge [Suf73] regarding polynomials with roots on the unit circle. In Suffridge’s result, qq is taken to be an element of the unit circle, and log mesh translates to mean that the roots are pairwise separated by at least the argument of qq. Roughly speaking, he obtains the same result for the corresponding qq-multiplicative convolution. Remarkably, the known proofs of his result (even a proof of Lamprecht) differ fairly substantially from Lamprecht’s proof of the above theorem.

Additionally, we note here that Lamprecht uses different notation and conventions in [Lam16]. In particular, he uses q∈(0,1)q\in(0,1), considers polynomials pp with all non-positive roots, and his definition of ⊠qn\boxtimes_{q}^{n} does not include the (−1)k(-1)^{k} factor. These differences are generally speaking unsubstantial, but it is worth noting that the arguments of §2 seem to require the (−1)k(-1)^{k} factor.

The bb-Additive Convolution

In this paper, we show the bb-additive convolution (or, finite difference convolution) preserves the space of polynomials with root mesh at least bb. Brändén, Krasikov, and Shapiro define the bb-additive convolution (only for b=1b=1) in [BKS16] as follows. (Note that as b→0b\to 0 this limits to the classical additive convolution.)

p⊞bnr:=∑k=0nΔbkp⋅(Δbn−kr)(0)p\boxplus_{b}^{n}r:=\sum_{k=0}^{n}\Delta_{b}^{k}p\cdot(\Delta_{b}^{n-k}r)(0)

Here, Δb\Delta_{b} is a finite bb-difference operator, defined as:

Δb:p↦p⁡(x)−p⁡(x−b)b\Delta_{b}:p\mapsto\frac{p(x)-p(x-b)}{b}

Our result then solves the first (and second) conjecture stated in [BKS16]. We state it formally here.

Definition 1.3.

Fix p∈ℝ⁡[x]p\in\mathbb{R}[x] with all real roots. We say that pp is bb-mesh if the minimum non-negative difference of any pair of roots of pp is at least bb. We also say that pp is strictly bb-mesh if this minimum difference is greater than bb. In these situations, we write mesh⁡(p)≥b\mesh(p)\geq b and mesh⁡(p)>b\mesh(p)>b respectively.

Theorem 1.4.

Let pp and rr be polynomials of degree at most nn such that mesh⁡(p)≥b\mesh(p)\geq b and mesh⁡(r)≥b\mesh(r)\geq b, for some b∈(0,∞)b\in(0,\infty). Then, mesh(p⊞bnr)≥b\mesh(p\boxplus_{b}^{n}r)\geq b.

As a note, Brändén, Krasikov, and Shapiro actually use the forward finite difference operator in their definition of the convolution. This is not a problem as our result then differs from their conjecture by a shift of the input polynomials.

Remark 1.5.

Although the qq-multiplicative and bb-additive convolutions preserve qq-log mesh and bb-mesh respectively, they do not preserve real-rootedness.

An Analytic Connection

Our first method of proof of Theorem 1.4 will demonstrate a way to pass root properties of the qq-multiplicative convolution to the bb-additive convolution. As this is interesting in its own right, we state the most general version of this result here.

Theorem 1.6.

Fix b≥0b\geq 0 and let p,rp,r be polynomials of degree nn. We have the following, where convergence is uniform on compact sets.

limq→1(1−q)n[Eq,b(p)⊠qbnEq,b(r)](qx)=p⊞bnr\lim_{q\rightarrow 1}(1-q)^{n}\left[E_{q,b}(p)\boxtimes_{q^{b}}^{n}E_{q,b}(r)\right](q^{x})=p\boxplus_{b}^{n}r

Note that for b=0b=0, this result pertains to the classical convolutions.

Here, the Eq,bE_{q,b} are certain linear isomorphisms of ℂ⁡[x]\mathbb{C}[x], to be explicitly defined below. Notice that uniform convergence allows us to use Hurwitz’ theorem to obtain root properties in the limit of the left-hand side. That is, any information about how the qq-multiplicative convolution acts on roots will transfer to some statement about how the bb-additive convolution acts on roots. As it turns out, a special case of Lamprecht’s result (Theorem 3 from [Lam16]) will become our result (Theorem 1.4) in the limit. We discuss this transfer process in more detail in §2.

Extending Lamprecht’s Method

Our second method of proof of Theorem 1.4 is an extension of the method used by Lamprecht to prove the log mesh result for the qq-multiplicative convolution. Specifically, he demonstrates that the qq-multiplicative convolution preserves a root-interlacing property for qq-log mesh polynomials. More formally he proves the following result which gives Theorem 1.4 as a corollary.

Theorem 1.7 (Lamprecht Interlacing-Preserving).

Let f,g∈ℝn​[x]f,g\in\mathbb{R}_{n}[x] be qq-log mesh polynomials of degree nn with only negative roots. Let Tg:ℝn​[x]→ℝn​[x]T_{g}:\mathbb{R}_{n}[x]\to\mathbb{R}_{n}[x] be the real linear operator defined by Tg:r↦r⊠qngT_{g}:r\mapsto r\boxtimes_{q}^{n}g. Then, TgT_{g} preserves the set of polynomials whose roots interlace the roots of ff.

We achieve an analogous result for the bb-additive convolution using techniques similar to those found in Lamprecht’s paper. We state it formally here.

Theorem 1.8.

Let f,g∈ℝn​[x]f,g\in\mathbb{R}_{n}[x] be bb-mesh polynomials of degree nn. Let Tg:ℝn​[x]→ℝn​[x]T_{g}:\mathbb{R}_{n}[x]\to\mathbb{R}_{n}[x] be the real linear operator defined by Tg:r↦r⊞bngT_{g}:r\mapsto r\boxplus_{b}^{n}g. Then, TgT_{g} preserves the set of polynomials whose roots interlace the roots of ff.

In both cases, mesh and log mesh properties can be shown to be equivalent to root interlacing properties (f⁡(x)f(x) interlaces f⁡(x−b)f(x-b) for bb-mesh, and f⁡(x)f(x) interlaces f⁡(q−1​x)f(q^{-1}x) for qq-log mesh). The above theorems then immediately imply the desired mesh preservation properties for the respective convolutions. We discuss this further in §3.

2 First Proof Method: The Finite Difference Convolution as a Limit of qq-Multiplicative Convolutions

In what follows we establish a general analytic connection between the multiplicative (Grace-Szego) and additive (Walsh) convolutions on polynomials of degree at most nn. We then extend this connection to the qq-multiplicative convolution and the bb-additive convolution (Theorem 1.6). Using this connection, we transfer root information results of the multiplicative convolution (qq or classical) to the additive convolution (bb or classical). Specifically, we use this connection to prove Theorem 1.4, which is the conjecture of Brändén, Krasikov, and Shapiro mentioned above.

To begin we state an observation of Vadim Gorin demonstrating an analytic connection in the classical case using matrix formulations of the classical convolutions given in [MSS15]:

χ⁡(A)⊠nχ⁡(B)=𝔼P[χ⁡(APBPT)]\chi(A)\boxtimes^{n}\chi(B)=\E_{P}\left[\chi(APBP^{T})\right]
χ(A)⊞nχ(B)=𝔼P[χ(A+PBPT)]\chi(A)\boxplus^{n}\chi(B)=\E_{P}\left[\chi(A+PBP^{T})\right]

Here, AA and BB are real symmetric matrices, χ\chi denotes the characteristic polynomial, and the expectations are taken over all permutation matrices. We then write:

limt→0t−n​[χ⁡(et​A)⊠nχ⁡(et​B)]​(t​x+1)=limt→0t−n​𝔼P[det(txI+I−etA​PetB​PT)]=limt→0t−n​𝔼P[det(txI−t⁡(APPT+PBPT)+O⁡(t2))]=limt→0𝔼P[χ⁡(A+PBPT+O⁡(t))]=χ(A)⊞nχ(B)\begin{split}\lim_{t\to 0}t^{-n}\left[\chi(e^{tA})\boxtimes^{n}\chi(e^{tB})\right](tx+1)&=\lim_{t\to 0}t^{-n}\E_{P}\left[\det\left(txI+I-e^{tA}Pe^{tB}P^{T}\right)\right]\\ &=\lim_{t\to 0}t^{-n}\E_{P}\left[\det\left(txI-t(APP^{T}+PBP^{T})+O(t^{2})\right)\right]\\ &=\lim_{t\to 0}\E_{P}\left[\chi\left(A+PBP^{T}+O(t)\right)\right]\\ &=\chi(A)\boxplus^{n}\chi(B)\end{split}

This connection is suggestive and straightforward, but seemingly confinded to the classical case. Therefore, we instead state below a slightly modified (but equivalent) version of this observation for the classical convolutions (Theorem 2.2) which we are able to then generalize to the qq-multiplicative and bb-additive convolutions.

2.1 The Classical Convolutions

We begin by sketching the proof of the connection between the classical additive and multiplicative convolutions. We then state rigorously the more general result for the qq-multiplicative and bb-additive convolutions. In this section, many quantities will be defined with b=0b=0 in mind (this corresponds to the classical additive convolution), with the more general quantities given in subsequent sections. Further, we will leave the proofs of the lemmas to the generic bb case, omitting them here.

To go from the multiplicative world to the additive world, we use a linear map which acts as an exponentiation on roots, and a limiting process which acts as a logarithm. In particular, we will refer to the following algebra endomorphism on ℂ⁡[x]\mathbb{C}[x] as our “exponential map”:

Eq,0:x↦1−x1−qE_{q,0}:x\mapsto\frac{1-x}{1-q}

In what follows, any limiting process will mean uniform convergence on compact sets in ℂ\mathbb{C}, unless otherwise specified. This will allow us to extract analytic information about roots using the classical Hurwitz’ theorem. In particular, the following result hints at the analytic information provided by the exponential map Eq,0E_{q,0}.

Proposition 2.1.

We have the following for any p∈ℂ⁡[x]p\in\mathbb{C}[x].

limq→1[Eq,0​(p)]​(qx)=p\lim_{q\rightarrow 1}[E_{q,0}(p)](q^{x})=p
Proof.

We first consider [Eq,0​(x)]​(qx)=1−qx1−q[E_{q,0}(x)](q^{x})=\frac{1-q^{x}}{1-q}, for which we obtain the following by the generalized binomial theorem:

limq→1[Eq,0​(x)]​(qx)=limq→11−qx1−q=limq→1∑m=1∞(xm)​(q−1)m−1=(x1)=x\lim_{q\to 1}[E_{q,0}(x)](q^{x})=\lim_{q\to 1}\frac{1-q^{x}}{1-q}=\lim_{q\to 1}\sum_{m=1}^{\infty}\binom{x}{m}(q-1)^{m-1}=\binom{x}{1}=x

To show that convergence here is uniform on compact sets, consider the tail for |x|≤M|x|\leq M:

|∑m=2∞(xm)​(q−1)m−1|≤∑m=0∞|(q−1)m+1⋅x(x−1)⋯(x−m−1)(m+2)!|≤|q−1|​∑m=0∞|q−1|m​∏k=1m+2(1+|x|k)≤|q−1|​(1+M)2​∑m=0∞(|q−1|​(1+M))m=|q−1|​(1+M)21−|q−1|(1+M)\begin{split}\left|\sum_{m=2}^{\infty}\binom{x}{m}(q-1)^{m-1}\right|&\leq\sum_{m=0}^{\infty}\left|(q-1)^{m+1}\cdot\frac{x(x-1)\cdots(x-m-1)}{(m+2)!}\right|\\ &\leq|q-1|\sum_{m=0}^{\infty}|q-1|^{m}\prod_{k=1}^{m+2}\left(1+\frac{|x|}{k}\right)\\ &\leq|q-1|(1+M)^{2}\sum_{m=0}^{\infty}\left(|q-1|(1+M)\right)^{m}\\ &=\frac{|q-1|(1+M)^{2}}{1-|q-1|(1+M)}\end{split}

This limits to zero as q→1q\to 1, which proves the desired convergence.

Since Eq,0E_{q,0} is an algebra morphism, we can use the fundamental theorem of algebra to complete the proof. Specifically, letting p⁡(x)=c0​∏k(x−αk)p(x)=c_{0}\prod_{k}(x-\alpha_{k}) we have:

limq→1[Eq,0​(c0​∏k(x−αk))]​(qx)=c0​∏k(limq→1[Eq,0​(x)]​(qx)−αk)=c0​∏k(x−αk)\lim_{q\to 1}\left[E_{q,0}\left(c_{0}\prod_{k}(x-\alpha_{k})\right)\right](q^{x})=c_{0}\prod_{k}\left(\lim_{q\to 1}[E_{q,0}(x)](q^{x})-\alpha_{k}\right)=c_{0}\prod_{k}(x-\alpha_{k})

∎

We now state our result in the classical case, which gives an analytic connection between the additive and multiplicative convolutions. As a note, many of the analytic arguments used in the proof of this result will have a flavor similar to that of the proof of Proposition 2.1.

Theorem 2.2.

Let p,r∈ℂ⁡[x]p,r\in\mathbb{C}[x] be of degree at most nn. We have the following.

limq→1(1−q)n[Eq,0(p)⊠nEq,0(r)](qx)=p⊞nr\lim_{q\rightarrow 1}(1-q)^{n}\left[E_{q,0}(p)\boxtimes^{n}E_{q,0}(r)\right](q^{x})=p\boxplus^{n}r

Proof Sketch

We will establish the above identity by calculating it on basis elements. Specifically, we will expand everything into powers of (1−q)(1-q). To prove the theorem, it then suffices to show that: (1) the negative degree coefficients are all zero, (2) the series has the desired constant term, and (3) the tail of the series converges to zero uniformly on compact sets. Our first step towards establishing this is expanding qk​xq^{kx} in terms of powers of (1−q)(1-q).

Remark 2.3.

Since we will only be considered with behavior for qq near 11, we will use the notation q≈1q\approx 1 to indicate there exists some ϵ>0\epsilon>0 such that the statement holds for q∈(1−ϵ,1+ϵ)q\in(1-\epsilon,1+\epsilon).

Definition 2.4.

We define a constant, which will help us to simplify the following computations.

αq,0:=ln⁡q1−q\alpha_{q,0}:=\frac{\ln q}{1-q}

Note that limq→1αq,0=−1\lim_{q\rightarrow 1}\alpha_{q,0}=-1.

Lemma 2.5.

Fix k∈ℕ0k\in\mathbb{N}_{0}. For q≈1q\approx 1, we have the following.

qk​x=∑m=0∞xmm!​αq,0m​km​(1−q)mq^{kx}=\sum_{m=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^{m}}{m!}\alpha_{q,0}^{m}k^{m}(1-q)^{m}

For fixed q≈1q\approx 1, this series has a finite radius of convergence, and this radius approaches infinity as q→1q\rightarrow 1.

Notice that this is not a true power series in (1−q)(1-q), as αq,0\alpha_{q,0} depends on qq. Using this, we can calculate the series obtained after plugging in specific basis elements.

Lemma 2.6.

Fix q≈1q\approx 1 in ℝ+\mathbb{R}_{+} and j,k,n∈ℕ0j,k,n\in\mathbb{N}_{0} such that 0≤j≤k≤n0\leq j\leq k\leq n. We have the following.

(1−q)n​[(1−x)j⊠n(1−x)k]​(qx)=∑m=0∞xmm!​αq,0m​(1−q)n+m−j−k​∑i=0j(ji)​(ki)(ni)​(−1)i​im(1-q)^{n}\left[(1-x)^{j}\boxtimes^{n}(1-x)^{k}\right](q^{x})=\sum_{m=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^{m}}{m!}\alpha_{q,0}^{m}(1-q)^{n+m-j-k}\sum_{i=0}^{j}\frac{\binom{j}{i}\binom{k}{i}}{\binom{n}{i}}(-1)^{i}i^{m}

We use interpolation arguments to handle the terms of this series, which are combinatorial in nature. In particular we show that this series has no nonzero negative degree terms, as seen in the following.

Proposition 2.7.

Fix j,k,m,n∈ℕ0j,k,m,n\in\mathbb{N}_{0} such that j≤kj\leq k and n+m−j−k≤0n+m-j-k\leq 0. We have the following identity.

∑i=0j(ji)​(ki)(ni)​(−1)i​im={(−1)n−j−k​(j)!​(k)!(n)!m=j+k−n0m<j+k−n\sum_{i=0}^{j}\frac{\binom{j}{i}\binom{k}{i}}{\binom{n}{i}}(-1)^{i}i^{m}=\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}(-1)^{n-j-k}\frac{(j)!(k)!}{(n)!}&m=j+k-n\\ 0&m<j+k-n\end{array}\right.

To deal with the tail of the series, we then use crude bounds to get uniform convergence on compact sets.

Lemma 2.8.

Fix M>0M>0, and j,k,n∈ℕ0j,k,n\in\mathbb{N}_{0} such that j≤k≤nj\leq k\leq n. For |x|≤M|x|\leq M, there exists γ>0\gamma>0 such that the following bound holds for q∈(1−γ,1+γ)q\in(1-\gamma,1+\gamma).

|∑m>j+k−nxmm!​αq,0m​(1−q)n+m−j−k​∑i=0j(ji)​(ki)(ni)​(−1)i​im|≤c0​c1​∑m=1∞c2m​|1−q|m\left|\sum_{m>j+k-n}\frac{x^{m}}{m!}\alpha_{q,0}^{m}(1-q)^{n+m-j-k}\sum_{i=0}^{j}\frac{\binom{j}{i}\binom{k}{i}}{\binom{n}{i}}(-1)^{i}i^{m}\right|\leq c_{0}c_{1}\sum_{m=1}^{\infty}c_{2}^{m}|1-q|^{m}

Here, c0,c1,c2c_{0},c_{1},c_{2} are independent of qq.

With this, we can now complete the proof of the theorem by comparing the desired quantity to the constant term in our series in (1−q)(1-q).

Proof of Theorem 2.2.

For j,k,n∈ℕ0j,k,n\in\mathbb{N}_{0} such that 0≤j≤k≤n0\leq j\leq k\leq n, we can combine the above results to obtain the following. Recall that limq→1αq,0=−1\lim_{q\rightarrow 1}\alpha_{q,0}=-1.

limq→1(1−q)n[(1−x)j⊠n(1−x)k](qx)=j!​k!n!​(j+k−n)!xj+k−n=xj⊞nxk\lim_{q\rightarrow 1}(1-q)^{n}\left[(1-x)^{j}\boxtimes^{n}(1-x)^{k}\right](q^{x})=\frac{j!k!}{n!(j+k-n)!}x^{j+k-n}=x^{j}\boxplus^{n}x^{k}

By symmetry, this demonstrates the desired result on a basis. Therefore, the proof is complete. ∎

2.2 General Connection Preliminaries

We now prove the previous results in more generality, which allows for extension to these generalized convolutions. First though, we give some preliminary notation.

Definition 2.9.

Fix q∈ℝ+q\in\mathbb{R}_{+} and x∈ℂx\in\mathbb{C}. We define (x)q:=1−qx1−q(x)_{q}:=\frac{1-q^{x}}{1-q}. Note that limq→1(x)q=x\lim_{q\rightarrow 1}(x)_{q}=x, using the generalized binomial theorem on qx=(1+(q−1))xq^{x}=(1+(q-1))^{x}.

Specifically, for any n∈ℤn\in\mathbb{Z}, we have:

(n)q:=1−qn1−q=1+q+q2+⋯+qn−1(n)_{q}:=\frac{1-q^{n}}{1-q}=1+q+q^{2}+\cdots+q^{n-1}

We then extend this notation to (n)q!:=(n)q(n−1)q⋯(2)q(1)q(n)_{q}!:=(n)_{q}(n-1)_{q}\cdots(2)_{q}(1)_{q} and (nk)q:=(n)q!(k)q!​(n−k)q!\binom{n}{k}_{q}:=\frac{(n)_{q}!}{(k)_{q}!(n-k)_{q}!}. We also define a system of bases of ℂ⁡[x]\mathbb{C}[x] which will help us to understand the mesh convolutions.

Definition 2.10.

For b≥0b\geq 0 and q∈ℝ+q\in\mathbb{R}_{+}, we define the following bases of ℂ⁡[x]\mathbb{C}[x].

vq,bk:=(1−x)(1−qbx)⋯(1−q(k−1)​bx)(1−q)kv_{q,b}^{k}:=\frac{(1-x)(1-q^{b}x)\cdots(1-q^{(k-1)b}x)}{(1-q)^{k}}
νbk:=x(x+b)(x+2b)⋯(x+(k−1)b)\nu_{b}^{k}:=x(x+b)(x+2b)\cdots(x+(k-1)b)

We demonstrate the relevance of these bases to the generalized convolutions by giving alternate definitions. Consider a linear map AbA_{b} on ℂ⁡[x]\mathbb{C}[x] defined via Ab:ν0k↦νbkA_{b}:\nu_{0}^{k}\mapsto\nu_{b}^{k}. That is, Ab:xk↦x⁡(x+b)​…​(x+(k−1)​b)A_{b}:x^{k}\mapsto x(x+b)\ldots(x+(k-1)b). We can then define the bb-additive convolution as follows:

p⊞bnr:=Ab(Ab−1(p)⊞nAb−1(r))p\boxplus_{b}^{n}r:=A_{b}(A_{b}^{-1}(p)\boxplus^{n}A_{b}^{-1}(r))

That is, the bb-additive convolution is essentially a change of basis of the classical additive convolution. Note that equivalently, one can conjugate ∂x\partial_{x} by AbA_{b} to obtain Δb:p↦p⁡(x)−p⁡(x−b)b\Delta_{b}:p\mapsto\frac{p(x)-p(x-b)}{b} which demonstrates the definition of ⊞bn\boxplus_{b}^{n} in terms of finite difference operators.

Similarly, the qq-multiplicative convolution can be seen as a change of basis of the classical multiplicative convolution. Consider a linear map Mq(n)M_{q}^{(n)} on ℂ⁡[x]\mathbb{C}[x] defined via Mq(n):(nk)​xk↦(nk)q​q(k2)​xkM_{q}^{(n)}:\binom{n}{k}x^{k}\mapsto\binom{n}{k}_{q}q^{\binom{k}{2}}x^{k}, which has the property that Mqb(n):(1−x)n↦(1−q)n​vq,bnM_{q^{b}}^{(n)}:(1-x)^{n}\mapsto(1-q)^{n}v_{q,b}^{n}. We can then define the qq-multiplicative convolution as follows:

p⊠qnr:=Mq(n)​((Mq(n))−1​(p)⊠n(Mq(n))−1​(r))p\boxtimes_{q}^{n}r:=M_{q}^{(n)}\left((M_{q}^{(n)})^{-1}(p)\boxtimes^{n}(M_{q}^{(n)})^{-1}(r)\right)

These bases will be used to simplify the proof of the general analytic connection for the mesh (non-classical) convolutions. In what follows they will play the role that the basis elements xkx^{k} and (1−x)k(1-x)^{k} did in the classical proof sketch above.

2.3 Main Result for Mesh Convolutions

We now generalize the results from the classical (b=0b=0) setting. First we define a generalized “exponential map” using the basis elements defined above. Note for b>0b>0 these are no longer algebra morphisms.

Eq,b:νbk↦vq,bkE_{q,b}:\nu_{b}^{k}\mapsto v_{q,b}^{k}

Notice that specialization to b=0b=0 recovers the original “exponential map”. Also notice that for any pp, the roots of Eq,b​(p)E_{q,b}(p) approach 1 as q→1q\to 1 (multiply the output polynomial by (1−q)deg⁡(p)(1-q)^{\deg(p)}). In all that follows, previously stated results can be immediately recovered by setting b=0b=0.

Proposition 2.11.

We obtain the same key relation for the generalized exponential maps:

limq→1[Eq,b​(p)]​(qx)=p\lim_{q\rightarrow 1}[E_{q,b}(p)](q^{x})=p
Proof.

We compute on basis elements, using Proposition 2.1 in the process:

limq→1[Eq,b​(νbk)]​(qx)=limq→1[vq,bk]​(qx)=limq→1(1−qx)(1−qx+b)⋯(1−qx+(k−1))(1−q)k=∏j=0k−1limq→11−qx+j​b1−q=∏j=0k−1(x+j​b)=νbk\begin{split}\lim_{q\rightarrow 1}[E_{q,b}(\nu_{b}^{k})](q^{x})&=\lim_{q\rightarrow 1}[v_{q,b}^{k}](q^{x})\\ &=\lim_{q\rightarrow 1}\frac{(1-q^{x})(1-q^{x+b})\cdots(1-q^{x+(k-1)})}{(1-q)^{k}}\\ &=\prod_{j=0}^{k-1}\lim_{q\rightarrow 1}\frac{1-q^{x+jb}}{1-q}=\prod_{j=0}^{k-1}(x+jb)=\nu_{b}^{k}\end{split}

∎

As in Proposition 2.1, one can interpret the Eq,bE_{q,b} maps as a way to exponentiate the roots of a polynomial. The inverse to these maps is given in the previous proposition by plugging in an exponential and limiting, which corresponds to taking the logarithm of the roots. This discussion will be made more precise in §2.4.

We now state and prove the main result, which gives an analytic link between the bb-additive and qq-multiplicative convolutions. We follow the proof sketch of the classical result given above, breaking the following full proof up into more manageable sections.

Theorem 1.6.

Fix b≥0b\geq 0 and let p,rp,r be polynomials of degree nn. We have the following.

limq→1(1−q)n[Eq,b(p)⊠qbnEq,b(r)](qx)=p⊞bnr\lim_{q\rightarrow 1}(1-q)^{n}\left[E_{q,b}(p)\boxtimes_{q^{b}}^{n}E_{q,b}(r)\right](q^{x})=p\boxplus_{b}^{n}r

Series Expansion

In order to prove this theorem, we first expand the left-hand side of the expression in a series in (1−q)m(1-q)^{m}. As above, this is not quite a power series in (1−q)m(1-q)^{m} as αq,b\alpha_{q,b} (which we now define) depends on qq.

Definition 2.12.

We define the bb-version of the αq,0\alpha_{q,0} constants as follows.

αq,b:={−(b)q−1q​bb>0ln⁡q1−qb=0\alpha_{q,b}:=\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}\frac{-(b)_{q^{-1}}}{qb}&b>0\\ \frac{\ln q}{1-q}&b=0\end{array}\right.

Note that limb→0αq,b=αq,0\lim_{b\rightarrow 0}\alpha_{q,b}=\alpha_{q,0} for q∈ℝ+q\in\mathbb{R}_{+}, and limq→1αq,b=−1\lim_{q\rightarrow 1}\alpha_{q,b}=-1 for fixed b≥0b\geq 0.

We now need to understand how exponential polynomials in qq relate to our basis elements.

Lemma 2.13.

Fix b≥0b\geq 0, and k∈ℕ0k\in\mathbb{N}_{0}. For q≈1q\approx 1 in ℝ+\mathbb{R}_{+}, we have the following.

qk​x=∑m=0∞νbmm!​αq,bm​(k)q−bm​(1−q)mq^{kx}=\sum_{m=0}^{\infty}\frac{\nu_{b}^{m}}{m!}\alpha_{q,b}^{m}(k)_{q^{-b}}^{m}(1-q)^{m}

For fixed q≈1q\approx 1, this series has a finite radius of convergence, and this radius approaches infinity as q→1q\rightarrow 1.

Proof.

For b>0b>0, we use the generalized binomial theorem to compute:

qk​x=(q−b​k−1+1)−x/b=∑m=0∞(−b)−mm!x(x+b)⋯(x+b(m−1))(q−b​k−1)m=∑m=0∞(−b)−m​νbmm!​(k)q−bm​(b)q−1m​(q−1−1)m=∑m=0∞νbmm!​(−(b)q−1q​b)m​(k)q−bm​(1−q)m\begin{split}q^{kx}=(q^{-bk}-1+1)^{-x/b}&=\sum_{m=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-b)^{-m}}{m!}x(x+b)\cdots(x+b(m-1))(q^{-bk}-1)^{m}\\ &=\sum_{m=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-b)^{-m}\nu_{b}^{m}}{m!}(k)_{q^{-b}}^{m}(b)_{q^{-1}}^{m}(q^{-1}-1)^{m}\\ &=\sum_{m=0}^{\infty}\frac{\nu_{b}^{m}}{m!}\left(-\frac{(b)_{q^{-1}}}{qb}\right)^{m}(k)_{q^{-b}}^{m}(1-q)^{m}\end{split}

For b=0b=0, manipulating the Taylor series of qk​x=ek​x​ln⁡qq^{kx}=e^{kx\ln q} gives the result.

For fixed q≈1q\approx 1, let δ>0\delta>0 be small enough such that |αq,b|<1+δq|\alpha_{q,b}|<\frac{1+\delta}{q} and (k)q−b<k+δ(k)_{q^{-b}}<k+\delta. Consider:

|νbm|=|x(x+b)⋯(x+(m−1)b)|≤m!(|x|+b)m|\nu_{b}^{m}|=|x(x+b)\cdots(x+(m-1)b)|\leq m!(|x|+b)^{m}

From this, we obtain:

|qk​x|≤∑m=0∞((|x|+b)​(1+δ)​(k+δ)q)m​|1−q|m|q^{kx}|\leq\sum_{m=0}^{\infty}\left(\frac{(|x|+b)(1+\delta)(k+\delta)}{q}\right)^{m}|1-q|^{m}

It is then easy to see that the radius of convergence of this series limits to infinity as q→1q\rightarrow 1. ∎

We will now proceed by proving the main result on a basis. To that end, we will prove a number of results related to basis element computations. Most of these are rather tedious and not very illuminating. Perhaps this can be simplified through some more detailed and generalized theory of qq- and bb-polynomial operators.

Lemma 2.14.

Fix q≈1q\approx 1 in ℝ+\mathbb{R}_{+}, b≥0b\geq 0, and j,k,n∈ℕ0j,k,n\in\mathbb{N}_{0} such that 0≤j≤k≤n0\leq j\leq k\leq n. We have the following.

(1−q)n​[vq,bj⊠qbnvq,bk]​(qx)=∑m=0∞νbmm!​αq,bm​(1−q)n+m−j−k​∑i=0j(ji)qb​(ki)qb(ni)qb​qb​i​(i−1)/2​(−1)i​(i)q−bm(1-q)^{n}\left[v_{q,b}^{j}\boxtimes_{q^{b}}^{n}v_{q,b}^{k}\right](q^{x})=\sum_{m=0}^{\infty}\frac{\nu_{b}^{m}}{m!}\alpha_{q,b}^{m}(1-q)^{n+m-j-k}\sum_{i=0}^{j}\frac{\binom{j}{i}_{q^{b}}\binom{k}{i}_{q^{b}}}{\binom{n}{i}_{q^{b}}}q^{bi(i-1)/2}(-1)^{i}(i)_{q^{-b}}^{m}
Proof.

We compute:

(1−q)n​[vq,bj⊠qbnvq,bk]​(qx)=(1−q)n−j−k​∑i=0j(ji)qb​(ki)qb(ni)qb​qb​i​(i−1)/2​(−1)i​qi​x=∑i=0j(ji)qb​(ki)qb(ni)qb​qb​i​(i−1)/2​(−1)i​∑m=0∞νbmm!​αq,bm​(1−q)n+m−j−k​(i)q−bm=∑m=0∞νbmm!​αq,bm​(1−q)n+m−j−k​∑i=0j(ji)qb​(ki)qb(ni)qb​qb​i​(i−1)/2​(−1)i​(i)q−bm\begin{split}(1-q)^{n}\left[v_{q,b}^{j}\boxtimes_{q^{b}}^{n}v_{q,b}^{k}\right](q^{x})&=(1-q)^{n-j-k}\sum_{i=0}^{j}\frac{\binom{j}{i}_{q^{b}}\binom{k}{i}_{q^{b}}}{\binom{n}{i}_{q^{b}}}q^{bi(i-1)/2}(-1)^{i}q^{ix}\\ &=\sum_{i=0}^{j}\frac{\binom{j}{i}_{q^{b}}\binom{k}{i}_{q^{b}}}{\binom{n}{i}_{q^{b}}}q^{bi(i-1)/2}(-1)^{i}\sum_{m=0}^{\infty}\frac{\nu_{b}^{m}}{m!}\alpha_{q,b}^{m}(1-q)^{n+m-j-k}(i)_{q^{-b}}^{m}\\ &=\sum_{m=0}^{\infty}\frac{\nu_{b}^{m}}{m!}\alpha_{q,b}^{m}(1-q)^{n+m-j-k}\sum_{i=0}^{j}\frac{\binom{j}{i}_{q^{b}}\binom{k}{i}_{q^{b}}}{\binom{n}{i}_{q^{b}}}q^{bi(i-1)/2}(-1)^{i}(i)_{q^{-b}}^{m}\end{split}

∎

Q-Lagrange Interpolation

To prove convergence in Theorem 1.6, we break up the infinite sum of Lemma 2.14 into two pieces. For n+m−j−k≤0n+m-j-k\leq 0, we use an interpolation argument to obtain the following identity. Note that this generalizes a similar identity (for q=1q=1) found in [Pet].

Proposition 2.15.

Fix q≈1q\approx 1, b≥0b\geq 0, and j,k,m,n∈ℕ0j,k,m,n\in\mathbb{N}_{0} such that j≤kj\leq k and n+m−k≤jn+m-k\leq j. We have the following identity.

∑i=0j(ji)qb​(ki)qb(ni)qb​qb​i​(i−1)/2​(−1)i​(i)q−bm={(−1)n−j−k​qb​(n2)−b​(j2)−b​(k2)​(j)qb!​(k)qb!(n)qb!m=j+k−n0m<j+k−n\sum_{i=0}^{j}\frac{\binom{j}{i}_{q^{b}}\binom{k}{i}_{q^{b}}}{\binom{n}{i}_{q^{b}}}q^{bi(i-1)/2}(-1)^{i}(i)_{q^{-b}}^{m}=\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}(-1)^{n-j-k}q^{b\binom{n}{2}-b\binom{j}{2}-b\binom{k}{2}}\frac{(j)_{q^{b}}!(k)_{q^{b}}!}{(n)_{q^{b}}!}&m=j+k-n\\ 0&m<j+k-n\end{array}\right.

[tj]​p​(t)=∑i=0jp⁡((i)q)​(−1)j−i(i)q!​(j−i)q!​q−(i2)​q−i⁡(j−i)[t^{j}]p(t)=\sum_{i=0}^{j}p((i)_{q})\frac{(-1)^{j-i}}{(i)_{q}!(j-i)_{q}!}q^{-\binom{i}{2}}q^{-i(j-i)}

Using the identity (i)q−1!=q−(i2)​(i)q!(i)_{q^{-1}}!=q^{-\binom{i}{2}}(i)_{q}! (via (i)q−1=q−i+1​(i)q(i)_{q^{-1}}=q^{-i+1}(i)_{q}) and replacing qq by q−1q^{-1} gives:

[tj]​p​(t)=∑i=0jp⁡((i)q−1)​(−1)j−i(i)q!​(j−i)q!​q2​(i2)​qi⁡(j−i)​q(j−i2)=∑i=0jp⁡((i)q−1)​(−1)j−i(i)q!​(j−i)q!​q(i2)​q(j2)\begin{split}[t^{j}]p(t)&=\sum_{i=0}^{j}p((i)_{q^{-1}})\frac{(-1)^{j-i}}{(i)_{q}!(j-i)_{q}!}q^{2\binom{i}{2}}q^{i(j-i)}q^{\binom{j-i}{2}}\\ &=\sum_{i=0}^{j}p((i)_{q^{-1}})\frac{(-1)^{j-i}}{(i)_{q}!(j-i)_{q}!}q^{\binom{i}{2}}q^{\binom{j}{2}}\end{split}

Proof of Proposition 2.15.

Consider the polynomial p(t)=tm((n)q−b−t)((n−1)q−b−t)⋯((k+1)q−b−t)p(t)=t^{m}((n)_{q^{-b}}-t)((n-1)_{q^{-b}}-t)\cdots((k+1)_{q^{-b}}-t), which is of degree m+n−k≤jm+n-k\leq j. Tail of the Series

For n+m−j−k>0n+m-j-k>0, we show that the tail of the infinite series in Lemma 2.14 is bounded by a geometric series in ϵ→0\epsilon\rightarrow 0 as q→1q\rightarrow 1. The proof, is somewhat similar to the discussion of convergence in the proof of Lemma 2.13.

Lemma 2.17.

Fix b≥0b\geq 0, M>0M>0, and j,k,n∈ℕ0j,k,n\in\mathbb{N}_{0} such that j≤k≤nj\leq k\leq n. For |x|≤M|x|\leq M, there exists γ>0\gamma>0 such that the following bound holds for q∈(1−γ,1+γ)q\in(1-\gamma,1+\gamma).

|∑m>j+k−nνbmm!​αq,bm​(1−q)n+m−j−k​∑i=0j(ji)qb​(ki)qb(ni)qb​qb​i​(i−1)/2​(−1)i​(i)q−bm|≤c0​c1​∑m=1∞c2m​|1−q|m\left|\sum_{m>j+k-n}\frac{\nu_{b}^{m}}{m!}\alpha_{q,b}^{m}(1-q)^{n+m-j-k}\sum_{i=0}^{j}\frac{\binom{j}{i}_{q^{b}}\binom{k}{i}_{q^{b}}}{\binom{n}{i}_{q^{b}}}q^{bi(i-1)/2}(-1)^{i}(i)_{q^{-b}}^{m}\right|\leq c_{0}c_{1}\sum_{m=1}^{\infty}c_{2}^{m}|1-q|^{m}

Here, c0,c1,c2c_{0},c_{1},c_{2} are independent of qq.

Proof.

Fix n+m−j−k>0n+m-j-k>0 with j≤k≤nj\leq k\leq n and q≈1q\approx 1. We have the following bound, where c0c_{0} is some positive constant independent of qq:

|∑i=0j(ji)qb​(ki)qb(ni)qb​qb​i​(i−1)/2​(−1)i​(i)q−bm|≤∑i=0jc0​(i+δ)m≤c0​(n+δ)m+1\left|\sum_{i=0}^{j}\frac{\binom{j}{i}_{q^{b}}\binom{k}{i}_{q^{b}}}{\binom{n}{i}_{q^{b}}}q^{bi(i-1)/2}(-1)^{i}(i)_{q^{-b}}^{m}\right|\leq\sum_{i=0}^{j}c_{0}(i+\delta)^{m}\leq c_{0}(n+\delta)^{m+1}

For |x|≤M|x|\leq M, we have:

|νbm|=|x(x+b)⋯(x+(m−1)b)|≤|M(M+b)⋯(M+(m−1)b)|≤m!(M+b)m|\nu_{b}^{m}|=|x(x+b)\cdots(x+(m-1)b)|\leq|M(M+b)\cdots(M+(m-1)b)|\leq m!(M+b)^{m}

This then implies the following bound on the tail. Let c1:=(n+δ)​[(1+δ)​(M+b)​(n+δ)]j+k−nc_{1}:=(n+\delta)\big[(1+\delta)(M+b)(n+\delta)\big]^{j+k-n} and c2:=(1+δ)​(M+b)​(n+δ)c_{2}:=(1+\delta)(M+b)(n+\delta), where small δ>0\delta>0 is needed to deal with limiting details.

|∑m=j+k+1−n∞νbmm!αq,bm(1−q)n+m−j−k∑i=0j(ji)qb​(ki)qb(ni)qbqb​i​(i−1)/2(−1)i(i)q−bm|≤∑m=j+k+1−n∞|νbmm!​αq,bm​(1−q)n+m−j−k|​c0​(n+δ)m+1≤c0​∑m=j+k+1−n∞(1+δ)m​(M+b)m​|1−q|n+m−j−k​(n+δ)m+1≤c0​c1​∑m=j+k+1−n∞[(1+δ)​(M+b)​(n+δ)​|1−q|]n+m−j−k=c0​c1​∑m=1∞c2m​|1−q|m\begin{split}\Bigg|\sum_{m=j+k+1-n}^{\infty}\frac{\nu_{b}^{m}}{m!}\alpha_{q,b}^{m}&(1-q)^{n+m-j-k}\sum_{i=0}^{j}\frac{\binom{j}{i}_{q^{b}}\binom{k}{i}_{q^{b}}}{\binom{n}{i}_{q^{b}}}q^{bi(i-1)/2}(-1)^{i}(i)_{q^{-b}}^{m}\Bigg|\\ &\leq\sum_{m=j+k+1-n}^{\infty}\left|\frac{\nu_{b}^{m}}{m!}\alpha_{q,b}^{m}(1-q)^{n+m-j-k}\right|c_{0}(n+\delta)^{m+1}\\ &\leq c_{0}\sum_{m=j+k+1-n}^{\infty}(1+\delta)^{m}(M+b)^{m}|1-q|^{n+m-j-k}(n+\delta)^{m+1}\\ &\leq c_{0}c_{1}\sum_{m=j+k+1-n}^{\infty}\big[(1+\delta)(M+b)(n+\delta)|1-q|\big]^{n+m-j-k}\\ &=c_{0}c_{1}\sum_{m=1}^{\infty}c_{2}^{m}|1-q|^{m}\end{split}

So, for any ϵ>0\epsilon>0 we can select qq close enough to 1 such that |1−q|<ϵc2|1-q|<\frac{\epsilon}{c_{2}}. This implies the above series is geometric with terms bounded by ϵm\epsilon^{m}.

∎

The above lemma in particular demonstrates that the tail of the series in Lemma 2.14 converges to 0 uniformly on compact sets. With this, we can now complete the proof of the theorem.

Proof of Theorem 1.6.

For j,k,n∈ℕ0j,k,n\in\mathbb{N}_{0} such that 0≤j≤k≤n0\leq j\leq k\leq n, we can combine the above results. When we expand our limit as a sum of powers of (1−q)(1-q), we have shown that everything limits to zero except for the constant term. Recall that limq→1αq,b=−1\lim_{q\rightarrow 1}\alpha_{q,b}=-1.

limq→1(1−q)n​[vq,bj⊠qbnvq,bk]​(qx)=limq→1νbj+k−n​αq,bj+k−n(j+k−n)!​(−1)j+k−n​qb​(n2)−b​(j2)−b​(k2)​(j)qb!​(k)qb!(n)qb!=j!​k!n!​(j+k−n)!​νbj+k−n=νbj⊞bnνbk\begin{split}\lim_{q\rightarrow 1}(1-q)^{n}\left[v_{q,b}^{j}\boxtimes_{q^{b}}^{n}v_{q,b}^{k}\right](q^{x})&=\lim_{q\to 1}\frac{\nu_{b}^{j+k-n}\alpha_{q,b}^{j+k-n}}{(j+k-n)!}(-1)^{j+k-n}q^{b\binom{n}{2}-b\binom{j}{2}-b\binom{k}{2}}\frac{(j)_{q^{b}}!(k)_{q^{b}}!}{(n)_{q^{b}}!}\\ &=\frac{j!k!}{n!(j+k-n)!}\nu_{b}^{j+k-n}\\ &=\nu_{b}^{j}\boxplus_{b}^{n}\nu_{b}^{k}\\ \end{split}

By symmetry, this demonstrates the desired result on a basis. Therefore, the proof is complete. ∎

2.4 Applications To Previous Results

The main motivation for the multiplicative to additive convolution connection was to be able to relate seemingly analogous root information results. The following table outlines the results we proceed to connect.

Additive Convolution Multiplicative Convolution
Preserves Real Rooted Polynomials Preserves Positive Rooted Polynomials
Additive Max Root Triangle Inequality Multiplicative Max Root Triangle Inequality
Preserves b−b-Mesh Preserves q−q-Logarithmic Mesh

All of these connections have a similar flavor, and rely on the following elementary facts about exponential polynomials. We say f⁡(x)=∑k=0nck​qk​xf(x)=\sum_{k=0}^{n}c_{k}q^{kx} is an exponential polynomial of degree nn with base qq. A real number xx is a root of ff if and only if qxq^{x} is a root of ∑k=0nck​xk\sum_{k=0}^{n}c_{k}x^{k}. Because of this we can bootstrap the fundamental theorem of algebra.

Definition 2.18.

We call {x∈ℂ:−π|ln⁡(q)|<ℑ⁡(x)<π|ln⁡(q)|}\left\{x\in\mathbb{C}:\frac{-\pi}{|\ln(q)|}<\Im(x)<\frac{\pi}{|\ln(q)|}\right\} the principal strip (with respect to qq). Let p⁡(qx)p(q^{x}) be an exponential polynomial of degree nn with base qq. The number of roots of p⁡(qx)p(q^{x}) in the principal strip is the same as the number of roots of pp in ℂ∖(−∞,0]\mathbb{C}\setminus(-\infty,0]. We call the roots in the principal strip the principal roots.

Lemma 2.19.

The principal roots of Eq,b​(p)​[qx]E_{q,b}(p)[q^{x}] converge to the roots of pp as q→1q\to 1. In particular, Eq,b​(p)​[qx]E_{q,b}(p)[q^{x}] has deg⁡(p)\deg(p) principal roots for q≈1q\approx 1.

Proof.

This follows from the fact that, as q→1q\to 1, Eq,b​(p)​[qx]E_{q,b}(p)[q^{x}] converges uniformly on compact sets to pp and the principal strip grows towards the whole plane. ∎

We can analyze the behavior of this convergence when pp is real rooted with distinct roots.

Lemma 2.20.

Suppose pp is real with real distinct roots. For q≈1q\approx 1, we have that Eq,b​(p)​[qx]E_{q,b}(p)[q^{x}] has principal roots which are real and distinct (and converging to the roots of pp).

Proof.

Since pp has real coefficients, the roots of Eq,b​(p)​[qx]E_{q,b}(p)[q^{x}] are either real or come in conjugate pairs. (Consider the fact that qx¯=qx¯q^{\overline{x}}=\overline{q^{x}}.) If pp has real distinct roots, the previous lemma implies the principal roots of Eq,b​(p)​[qx]E_{q,b}(p)[q^{x}] have distinct real part for qq close enough to 1. Therefore, the principal roots of Eq,b​(p)​[qx]E_{q,b}(p)[q^{x}] must all be real. ∎

If we exponentiate (with base qq) the principal roots of Eq,b​(p)​[qx]E_{q,b}(p)[q^{x}], we get the roots of Eq,b​(p)E_{q,b}(p). So if the principal roots of Eq,b​(p)​[qx]E_{q,b}(p)[q^{x}] are real, then the roots of Eq,b​(p)E_{q,b}(p) are positive. Considering the above results, this means that Eq,bE_{q,b} maps polynomials with distinct real roots to polynomials with distinct positive roots for q≈1q\approx 1. (In fact, the roots will be near 1.)

Root Preservation

The most classical results about the roots are the following:

Theorem (Root Preservation).
  • •

    If p,r∈ℝn​[x]p,r\in\mathbb{R}_{n}[x] have positive roots, then p⊠nrp\boxtimes^{n}r has positive roots.

  • •

    If p,r∈ℝn​[x]p,r\in\mathbb{R}_{n}[x] have real roots, then p⊞nrp\boxplus^{n}r has real roots.

Neither of these results are particularly hard to prove, but showing how the additive result follows from the multiplicative serves as a prime example of how our theorem connects results on the roots.

Proof of Additive from Multiplicative.

We can reduce to showing that the additive convolution preserves real rooted polynomials with distinct roots since the closure of polynomials with distinct real roots is all real rooted polynomials.

By Lemma 2.20, the roots of Eq,0​(p)E_{q,0}(p) are real, distinct, and exponentials of the principal roots of Eq,0​[p]​(qx)E_{q,0}[p](q^{x}) for q≈1q\approx 1. This implies that Eq,0​(p)E_{q,0}(p) has positive real roots. By the multiplicative result, Eq,0​(p)⊠nEq,0​(r)E_{q,0}(p)\boxtimes^{n}E_{q,0}(r) has positive real roots, and therefore [Eq,0​(p)⊠nEq,0​(r)]​(qx)[E_{q,0}(p)\boxtimes^{n}E_{q,0}(r)](q^{x}) has real principal roots. By our main result, (1−q)n​[Eq,0​(p)⊠nEq,0​(r)]​(qx)(1-q)^{n}[E_{q,0}(p)\boxtimes^{n}E_{q,0}(r)](q^{x}) converges to p⊞nrp\boxplus^{n}r. The real-rootedness of [Eq,0​(p)⊠nEq,0​(r)]​(qx)[E_{q,0}(p)\boxtimes^{n}E_{q,0}(r)](q^{x}) for q≈1q\approx 1 then implies p⊞nrp\boxplus^{n}r is real-rooted. ∎

Triangle Inequality

The next classical theorem relates to the max root of a given polynomial. Given a real-rooted polynomial pp, let λ⁡(p)\lambda({p}) denote its max root. Given an exponential polynomial ff with principal roots all real, let λ⁡(f)\lambda({f}) denote the largest principal root of ff. Also, denote expq⁡(α):=qα\exp_{q}(\alpha):=q^{\alpha}.

Theorem (Triangle Inequalities).
  • •

    Given positive-rooted polynomials p,rp,r we have λ⁡(p⊠nr)≤λ⁡(p)⋅λ⁡(r)\lambda({p\boxtimes^{n}r})\leq\lambda({p})\cdot\lambda({r})

  • •

    Given real-rooted polynomials p,rp,r we have λ(p⊞nr)≤λ(p)+λ(r)\lambda({p\boxplus^{n}r})\leq\lambda({p})+\lambda({r})

As before, neither of these have particularly complicated proofs, but we can use the multiplicative result to deduce the additive result in the following.

Proof of Additive from Multiplicative.

As in the previous proof, we can reduce to showing that the result holds for p,rp,r with distinct roots. For this proof, we only consider q>1q>1.

By Lemma 2.20, we have that the roots of Eq,0​(p)E_{q,0}(p) are real, distinct, and exponentials of the principal roots of Eq,0​[p]​(qx)E_{q,0}[p](q^{x}) for q≈1q\approx 1. This implies the roots of Eq,0​(p)E_{q,0}(p) are positive for q≈1q\approx 1. Additionally, notice that expq⁡(λ⁡(f⁡(qx)))=λ⁡(f⁡(p))\exp_{q}(\lambda(f(q^{x})))=\lambda(f(p)) whenever ff is positive-rooted. From the multiplicative result and the fact that ⊠n\boxtimes^{n} preserves positive-rootednes, we have the following for q≈1q\approx 1:

expq⁡(λ⁡([Eq,0​(p)⊠nEq,0​(r)]​(qx)))=λ⁡(Eq,0​(p)⊠nEq,0​(r))≤λ⁡(Eq,0​(p))⋅λ⁡(Eq,0​(r))=expq⁡(λ⁡(Eq,0​[p]​(qx))+λ⁡(Eq,0​[r]​(qx)))\begin{split}\exp_{q}(\lambda([E_{q,0}(p)\boxtimes^{n}E_{q,0}(r)](q^{x})))&=\lambda({E_{q,0}(p)\boxtimes^{n}E_{q,0}(r)})\\ &\leq\lambda({E_{q,0}(p)})\cdot\lambda({E_{q,0}(r)})\\ &=\exp_{q}(\lambda({E_{q,0}[p](q^{x})})+\lambda({E_{q,0}[r](q^{x})}))\end{split}

Therefore, λ⁡([Eq,0​(p)⊠nEq,0​(r)]​(qx))≤λ⁡(Eq,0​[p]​(qx))+λ⁡(Eq,0​[r]​(qx))\lambda([E_{q,0}(p)\boxtimes^{n}E_{q,0}(r)](q^{x}))\leq\lambda(E_{q,0}[p](q^{x}))+\lambda(E_{q,0}[r](q^{x})). By our main result, (1−q)n​[Eq,0​(p)⊠nEq,0​(r)]​(qx)(1-q)^{n}[E_{q,0}(p)\boxtimes^{n}E_{q,0}(r)](q^{x}) converges to p⊞nrp\boxplus^{n}r, and therefore λ⁡([Eq,0​(p)⊠nEq,0​(r)]​(qx))\lambda([E_{q,0}(p)\boxtimes^{n}E_{q,0}(r)](q^{x})) converges to λ(p⊞nr)\lambda(p\boxplus^{n}r). Similarly λ⁡(Eq,0​[p]​(qx))\lambda({E_{q,0}[p](q^{x})}) converges to λ⁡(p)\lambda({p}), and the result follows. ∎

Application to Mesh Preservation Conjecture

Recall the log mesh result of Lamprecht in [Lam16] regarding the qq-multiplicative convolution.

Theorem 1.2.

Fix q>1q>1. Given positive-rooted polynomials p,r∈ℝn​[x]p,r\in\mathbb{R}_{n}[x] with lmesh⁡(p),lmesh⁡(r)≥q\lmesh(p),\lmesh(r)\geq q, we have:

lmesh⁡(p⊠qnr)≥q\lmesh(p\boxtimes_{q}^{n}r)\geq q

In [BKS16], Brändén, Krasikov, and Shapiro conjectured the analogous result for the bb-additive convolution (for b=1b=1). Using our connection we will confirm this conjecture:

Theorem 1.4.

Given real-rooted polynomials p,r∈ℝn​[x]p,r\in\mathbb{R}_{n}[x] with mesh⁡(p),mesh⁡(r)≥b\mesh(p),\mesh(r)\geq b, we have:

mesh(p⊞bnr)≥bmesh(p\boxplus_{b}^{n}r)\geq b
Proof.

We will prove this claim for polynomials p,rp,r with mesh⁡(p),mesh⁡(r)>b\mesh(p),\mesh(r)>b. Since we can approximate any polynomial with mesh⁡(p)=b\mesh(p)=b by polynomials with larger mesh, the result then follows.

By Lemma 2.20, Eq,b​[p]​(qx)E_{q,b}[p](q^{x}) has real roots which converge to the roots of pp for q≈1q\approx 1. Since the roots of pp satisfy mesh⁡(p)>b\mesh(p)>b, the principal roots of Eq,b​[p]​(qx)E_{q,b}[p](q^{x}) will have mesh greater than bb for q≈1q\approx 1. Further, lmesh⁡(Eq,b​(p))=expq⁡(mesh⁡(Eq,b​[p]​(qx)))>qb\lmesh(E_{q,b}(p))=\exp_{q}(\mesh(E_{q,b}[p](q^{x})))>q^{b}. (All of this discussion holds for rr as well.) By our main result, we have:

limq→1(1−q)n[Eq,b(p)⊠qbnEq,b(r)](qx)=p⊞bnr\lim_{q\rightarrow 1}(1-q)^{n}\left[E_{q,b}(p)\boxtimes_{q^{b}}^{n}E_{q,b}(r)\right](q^{x})=p\boxplus_{b}^{n}r

By the previous theorem, the qbq^{b}-multiplicative convolution of Eq,b​(p)E_{q,b}(p) and Eq,b​(r)E_{q,b}(r) has logarithmic mesh at least qbq^{b}. Precomposition by qxq^{x} then yields an exponential polynomial with mesh (of the principal roots) at least bb. The principal roots of this exponential polynomial then converge to p⊞bnrp\boxplus_{b}^{n}r, and hence p⊞bnrp\boxplus_{b}^{n}r has mesh at least bb. ∎

3 Second Proof Method: A Direct Proof using Interlacing

While the previous framework generically transferred Lamprecht’s multiplicative result to prove the conjectured result in the additive realm, one might desire a direct proof to gain insight on the underlying structure of the convolution. In what follows, we first outline the preliminary knowledge required to understand a special case of Lamprecht’s argument. Then we outline his approach in the multiplicative case and extend this approach to the additive realm to prove the desired conjecture.

3.1 Interlacing Preserving Operators

Given f,g∈ℝ⁡[x]f,g\in\mathbb{R}[x], we say f≪gf\ll g iff f′​g−f​g′≤0f^{\prime}g-fg^{\prime}\leq 0 iff (fg)′≤0\left(\frac{f}{g}\right)^{\prime}\leq 0 wherever defined. Further, we say f≪gf\ll g strictly iff f′​g−f​g′<0f^{\prime}g-fg^{\prime}<0. Additionally, it is well known that ff and gg are real-rooted with interlacing roots iff f≪gf\ll g or g≪fg\ll f. Further, ff and gg have strictly interlacing roots (no shared roots) iff f≪gf\ll g strictly or g≪fg\ll f strictly.

Let λf\lambda_{f} denote the largest root of ff. If ff and gg are monic, then f≪gf\ll g implies λf≤λg\lambda_{f}\leq\lambda_{g}. We give a short proof of this now. If ff has a double root at λf\lambda_{f}, then interlacing implies g⁡(λf)=0g(\lambda_{f})=0, and therefore λf≤λg\lambda_{f}\leq\lambda_{g}. Otherwise, consider that f≪gf\ll g implies f′​(λf)⋅g⁡(λf)=(f′​g−f​g′)​(λf)≤0f^{\prime}(\lambda_{f})\cdot g(\lambda_{f})=(f^{\prime}g-fg^{\prime})(\lambda_{f})\leq 0. Since ff is monic, we have f′​(λf)>0f^{\prime}(\lambda_{f})>0 which in turn implies g⁡(λf)≤0g(\lambda_{f})\leq 0. Since gg is monic, this implies the result. Note that this further implies that if ff and gg are monic and deg⁡(f)=deg⁡(g)−1\deg(f)=\deg(g)-1, then ff and gg have interlacing roots iff f≪gf\ll g.

Another classical result allows us to combine interlacing relations. If f≪gf\ll g and f≪hf\ll h, then f≪a​g+b​hf\ll ag+bh for any a,b∈ℝ+a,b\in\mathbb{R}_{+}. A similar result holds if g≪fg\ll f and h≪fh\ll f. Note also that f≪gf\ll g iff g≪−fg\ll-f, and that a​f≪b​faf\ll bf for all a,b∈ℝa,b\in\mathbb{R}. Finally, the Hermite-Biehler theorem says a​f+b​gaf+bg is real-rooted for all a,b∈ℝa,b\in\mathbb{R} iff either f≪gf\ll g or g≪fg\ll f.

Remark 3.1.

A polynomial ff with non-negative roots is qq-log mesh if and only if f≪f⁡(q−1​x)f\ll f(q^{-1}x) and strictly qq-log mesh if and only if f≪f⁡(q−1​x)f\ll f(q^{-1}x) strictly (for q>1q>1). Similarly, a polynomial ff with real roots is bb-mesh if and only if f≪f⁡(x−b)f\ll f(x-b) and strictly bb-mesh if and only if f≪f⁡(x−b)f\ll f(x-b) strictly (for b>0b>0).

Now let ff and gg be of degree nn, and suppose ff has nn simple real roots, α1,…,αn\alpha_{1},...,\alpha_{n}. By partial fraction decomposition, we have:

g⁡(x)f⁡(x)=c+∑k=1ncαkx−αk\frac{g(x)}{f(x)}=c+\sum_{k=1}^{n}\frac{c_{\alpha_{k}}}{x-\alpha_{k}}

Denoting fαk​(x):=f⁡(x)(x−αk)f_{\alpha_{k}}(x):=\frac{f(x)}{(x-\alpha_{k})}, this implies:

g⁡(x)=c​f​(x)+∑k=1ncαk​fαk​(x)g(x)=cf(x)+\sum_{k=1}^{n}c_{\alpha_{k}}f_{\alpha_{k}}(x)

If g⁡(αk)=0g(\alpha_{k})=0, then cαk=0c_{\alpha_{k}}=0. Otherwise we compute:

cαk=limx→αk(x−αk)​g​(x)f⁡(x)=[f′​(αk)g⁡(αk)]−1=[(fg)′​(αk)]−1c_{\alpha_{k}}=\lim_{x\to\alpha_{k}}\frac{(x-\alpha_{k})g(x)}{f(x)}=\left[\frac{f^{\prime}(\alpha_{k})}{g(\alpha_{k})}\right]^{-1}=\left[\left(\frac{f}{g}\right)^{\prime}(\alpha_{k})\right]^{-1}

This leads to the first result, which is a classical one.

Proposition 3.2.

Fix f,g∈ℝn​[x]f,g\in\mathbb{R}_{n}[x]. Suppose ff is monic and has nn simple real roots, α1,…,αn\alpha_{1},...,\alpha_{n}. Consider the decomposition:

g⁡(x)=c​f​(x)+∑k=1ncαk​fαk​(x)g(x)=cf(x)+\sum_{k=1}^{n}c_{\alpha_{k}}f_{\alpha_{k}}(x)

Then, g≪fg\ll f iff cαk≥0c_{\alpha_{k}}\geq 0 for all kk, and f≪gf\ll g iff cαk≤0c_{\alpha_{k}}\leq 0 for all kk.

Proof.

(⇒)(\Rightarrow). If f≪gf\ll g, then (fg)′≤0\left(\frac{f}{g}\right)^{\prime}\leq 0. This implies cαk≤0c_{\alpha_{k}}\leq 0 for all kk. If g≪fg\ll f, then f≪−gf\ll-g. The same argument implies cαk≥0c_{\alpha_{k}}\geq 0 for all kk.

(⇐)(\Leftarrow). By the above argument, c​f≪fcf\ll f and fαk≪ff_{\alpha_{k}}\ll f for all kk. So, if cαk≥0c_{\alpha_{k}}\geq 0 for all kk, then:

g=c​f+∑k=1ncαk​fαk​(x)≪fg=cf+\sum_{k=1}^{n}c_{\alpha_{k}}f_{\alpha_{k}}(x)\ll f

A similar argument works to show f≪gf\ll g if cαk≤0c_{\alpha_{k}}\leq 0 for all kk. ∎

There is actually another way to state this result, in terms of cones of polynomials. Let cone⁡(f1,…,fm)\cone(f_{1},...,f_{m}) denote the closure of the positive cone generated by the polynomials f1,…,fmf_{1},...,f_{m}.

Corollary 3.3.

Let f∈ℝn​[x]f\in\mathbb{R}_{n}[x] be a monic polynomial with nn simple roots, α1,…,αn\alpha_{1},...,\alpha_{n}. Then, {g∈ℝn​[x]:g≪f}=cone⁡(f,−f,fα1,…,fαn)\{g\in\mathbb{R}_{n}[x]:g\ll f\}=\cone(f,-f,f_{\alpha_{1}},...,f_{\alpha_{n}}) and {g∈ℝn​[x]:f≪g}=cone⁡(f,−f,−fα1,…,−fαn)\{g\in\mathbb{R}_{n}[x]:f\ll g\}=\cone(f,-f,-f_{\alpha_{1}},...,-f_{\alpha_{n}}).

Proof.

Since any g∈ℝn​[x]g\in\mathbb{R}_{n}[x] can be written as a linear combination of f,fα1,…,fαnf,f_{\alpha_{1}},...,f_{\alpha_{n}}, the result follows from the previous proposition. ∎

This immediately yields the following result concerning linear operators preserving certain interlacing relations.

Definition 3.4.

Given a real linear operator T:ℝn​[x]→ℝ​[x]T:\mathbb{R}_{n}[x]\to\mathbb{R}[x], and a real-rooted polynomial ff, we say that TT preserves interlacing with respect to ff if g≪fg\ll f implies T⁡[g]≪T⁡[f]T[g]\ll T[f] and f≪gf\ll g implies T⁡[f]≪T⁡[g]T[f]\ll T[g] for all g∈ℝn​[x]g\in\mathbb{R}_{n}[x]

Corollary 3.5.

Fix a real linear operator T:ℝn​[x]→ℝ​[x]T:\mathbb{R}_{n}[x]\to\mathbb{R}[x], and fix f∈ℝn​[x]f\in\mathbb{R}_{n}[x]. Suppose ff is monic with nn simple roots, α1,…,αn\alpha_{1},...,\alpha_{n}, and that T⁡[fαk]≪T⁡[f]T[f_{\alpha_{k}}]\ll T[f] for all kk. Then, TT preserves interlacing with respect to ff.

3.2 Lamprecht’s Approach

In what follows, we follow Lamprecht’s approach to proving that the space of qq-log mesh polynomials is preserved by the qq-mutliplicative convolution. Here, we are only interested in proving this result for qq-log mesh polynomials with non-negative roots, which simplifies the proof. (Lamprecht demonstrates this result for a more general class of polynomials.) The main structure of the proof is: (1) establish properties of two distinguished polar derivatives, (2) show how these derivatives relate to the qq-multiplicative convolution, and (3) use this to prove that the qq-multiplicative convolution preserves certain interlacing properties. In the next section, we will emulate this method for bb-mesh polynomials and the bb-additive convolution.

qq-Polar Derivatives

In [Lam16], Lamprecht defines the following qq-derivative operators, which generalize the operators ∂x\partial_{x} and −∂y-\partial_{y} on homogeneous polynomials. Here, q>1q>1 is always assumed, as above. (As a note, Lamprecht uses the Δ\Delta symbol for these derivatives, and actually gives different definitions as his convention is q∈(0,1)q\in(0,1).)

(dq,n​f)​(x):=f⁡(q​x)−f⁡(x)q1−n​(qn−1)​x(dq,n∗​f)​(x):=f⁡(q​x)−qn​f​(x)qn−1(d_{q,n}f)(x):=\frac{f(qx)-f(x)}{q^{1-n}(q^{n}-1)x}~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~(d_{q,n}^{*}f)(x):=\frac{f(qx)-q^{n}f(x)}{q^{n}-1}

He then goes on to show that these “derivative” operators have similar preservation properties to that of the usual derivatives. In particular, he obtains the following.

Proposition 3.6.

The operators dq,n:ℝn​[x]→ℝn−1​[x]d_{q,n}:\mathbb{R}_{n}[x]\to\mathbb{R}_{n-1}[x] and dq,n∗:ℝn​[x]→ℝn−1​[x]d_{q,n}^{*}:\mathbb{R}_{n}[x]\to\mathbb{R}_{n-1}[x] preserve the space of qq-log mesh polynomials and the space of strictly qq-log mesh polynomials. Further, we have that dq,n​f≪fd_{q,n}f\ll f and dq,n∗​f≪dq,n​fd_{q,n}^{*}f\ll d_{q,n}f.

The above result is actually spread across a number of results in Lamprecht’s paper. We omit the proof for now, referring the reader to [Lam16].

Recursive Identities

Lamprecht then determines the following identities, which are crucial to his inductive proof of the main result of this section. Fix f∈ℝn−1​[x]f\in\mathbb{R}_{n-1}[x] and g∈ℝn​[x]g\in\mathbb{R}_{n}[x].

f⊠qng=f⊠qn−1dq,n∗​g(x​f)⊠qng=x⁡(f⊠qn−1dq,n​g)f\boxtimes_{q}^{n}g=f\boxtimes_{q}^{n-1}d_{q,n}^{*}g~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~(xf)\boxtimes_{q}^{n}g=x(f\boxtimes_{q}^{n-1}d_{q,n}g)

Lamprecht’s Proof

With this, we now state an interesting result about interlacing preservation of the qq-convolution operator. We will then derive the main result as a corollary.

Theorem 1.7 (Lamprecht Interlacing-Preserving).

Let f,g∈ℝn​[x]f,g\in\mathbb{R}_{n}[x] be qq-log mesh polynomials of degree nn with only positive roots. Let Tg:ℝn​[x]→ℝn​[x]T_{g}:\mathbb{R}_{n}[x]\to\mathbb{R}_{n}[x] be the real linear operator defined by Tg:r↦r⊠qngT_{g}:r\mapsto r\boxtimes_{q}^{n}g. Then, TgT_{g} preserves interlacing with respect to ff.

Proof.

We prove the theorem by induction. For n=1n=1 the result is straightforward, as ⊠q1≡⊠1\boxtimes_{q}^{1}\equiv\boxtimes^{1}. For m>1m>1, we inductively assume that the result holds for n=m−1n=m-1. By Corollary 3.5 and the fact that ff has nn simple roots, we only need to show that Tg​[fαk]≪Tg​[f]T_{g}[f_{\alpha_{k}}]\ll T_{g}[f] for all roots αk\alpha_{k} of ff. That is, we want to show fαk⊠qmg≪f⊠qmgf_{\alpha_{k}}\boxtimes_{q}^{m}g\ll f\boxtimes_{q}^{m}g for all kk.

By Proposition 3.6, we have that dq,m​gd_{q,m}g and dq,m∗​gd_{q,m}^{*}g are qq-log mesh and dq,m∗​g≪dq,m​gd_{q,m}^{*}g\ll d_{q,m}g. Further, dq,m​gd_{q,m}g and dq,m∗​gd_{q,m}^{*}g are of degree m−1m-1 and have no roots at 0. The inductive hypothesis and symmetry of ⊠qn\boxtimes_{q}^{n} then imply:

fαk⊠qm−1dq,m∗​g≪fαk⊠qm−1dq,m​gf_{\alpha_{k}}\boxtimes_{q}^{m-1}d^{*}_{q,m}g\ll f_{\alpha_{k}}\boxtimes_{q}^{m-1}d_{q,m}g

The fact that these polynomial have leading coefficients with the same sign means that the max root of fαk⊠qm−1dq,m​gf_{\alpha_{k}}\boxtimes_{q}^{m-1}d_{q,m}g is larger than that of fαk⊠qm−1dq,m∗​gf_{\alpha_{k}}\boxtimes_{q}^{m-1}d^{*}_{q,m}g. Further, since all roots are positive we obtain:

fαk⊠qm−1dq,m∗​g≪x⁡(fαk⊠qm−1dq,m​g)f_{\alpha_{k}}\boxtimes_{q}^{m-1}d_{q,m}^{*}g\ll x(f_{\alpha_{k}}\boxtimes_{q}^{m-1}d_{q,m}g)

By properties of ≪\ll, this gives:

fαk⊠qm−1dq,m∗​g≪x⁡(fαk⊠qm−1dq,m​g)−αk​(fαk⊠qm−1dq,m∗​g)f_{\alpha_{k}}\boxtimes_{q}^{m-1}d_{q,m}^{*}g\ll x(f_{\alpha_{k}}\boxtimes_{q}^{m-1}d_{q,m}g)-\alpha_{k}(f_{\alpha_{k}}\boxtimes_{q}^{m-1}d_{q,m}^{*}g)

By the above identities and the fact that f⁡(x)=(x−αk)​fαk​(x)f(x)=(x-\alpha_{k})f_{\alpha_{k}}(x), this is equivalent to fαk⊠qmg≪f⊠qmgf_{\alpha_{k}}\boxtimes_{q}^{m}g\ll f\boxtimes_{q}^{m}g. ∎

Corollary 1.2.

Let f,g∈ℝn​[x]f,g\in\mathbb{R}_{n}[x] be qq-log mesh polynomials (with non-negative roots), not necessarily of degree nn. Then, f⊠qngf\boxtimes_{q}^{n}g is qq-log mesh.

Proof.

First suppose f,gf,g are of degree nn with only positive roots. Since f≪f⁡(q−1​x)f\ll f(q^{-1}x), the previous theorem implies:

f⊠qng≪f⁡(q−1​x)⊠qng=(f⊠qng)​(q−1​x)f\boxtimes_{q}^{n}g\ll f(q^{-1}x)\boxtimes_{q}^{n}g=(f\boxtimes_{q}^{n}g)(q^{-1}x)

That is, f⊠qngf\boxtimes_{q}^{n}g is qq-log mesh.

Otherwise, suppose ff is of degree mf≤nm_{f}\leq n with zfz_{f} roots at 0 and gg is of degree mg≤nm_{g}\leq n with zgz_{g} roots at zero. Intuitively, we now add roots “near 0 and ∞\infty” and limit. Let new polynomials FF and GG be given as follows:

F(x):=f(x)⋅x−zf∏j=1zf(x−1αj)⋅∏j=mf+1n(xαj−1)F(x):=f(x)\cdot x^{-z_{f}}\prod_{j=1}^{z_{f}}\left(x-\frac{1}{\alpha_{j}}\right)\cdot\prod_{j=m_{f}+1}^{n}\left(\frac{x}{\alpha_{j}}-1\right)
G(x):=g(x)⋅x−zg∏j=1zg(x−1βj)⋅∏j=mg+1n(xβj−1)G(x):=g(x)\cdot x^{-z_{g}}\prod_{j=1}^{z_{g}}\left(x-\frac{1}{\beta_{j}}\right)\cdot\prod_{j=m_{g}+1}^{n}\left(\frac{x}{\beta_{j}}-1\right)

Here, αj\alpha_{j} and βj\beta_{j} are any large positive numbers such that FF and GG are qq-log mesh polynomials of degree nn. By the previous argument, F⊠qnGF\boxtimes_{q}^{n}G is qq-log mesh. Letting αj\alpha_{j} and βj\beta_{j} limit to ∞\infty (while preserving qq-log mesh) implies F⊠qnG→f⊠qngF\boxtimes_{q}^{n}G\to f\boxtimes_{q}^{n}g root-wise, which implies f⊠qngf\boxtimes_{q}^{n}g is qq-log mesh. ∎

Lamprecht is actually able to remove the degree nn with positive roots restriction earlier in the line of argument, albeit at the cost of a more complicated proof. We have elected here to take the simpler route. He also proves similar results for a class of qq-log mesh polynomials with possibly negative roots, which we omit here.

3.3 bb-Additive Convolution

The main structure of Lamprecht’s argument revolves around the two “polar” qq-derivatives, dq,nd_{q,n} and dq,n∗d_{q,n}^{*}. The key properties of these derivatives are: (1) they preserve the space of qq-log mesh polynomials, and (2) they recursively work well with the definition of the qq-multiplicative convolution. So, when extending this argument to the bb-additive convolution we face an immediate problem: there is only one natural derivative which preserves the space of bb-mesh polynomials. This stems from the fact that 0 and ∞\infty have special roles in the qq-multiplicative world, whereas only ∞\infty is special in the bb-additive world. The key idea we introduce then is that given a fixed bb-mesh polynomial ff, we can pick a polar derivative with pole “close enough to ∞\infty” so that it maps ff to a bb-mesh polynomial. The fact that we use a different polar derivative for each fixed input ff does not affect the proof method.

We now give a few facts about the finite difference operator Δb\Delta_{b}, which plays a crucial role in the definition of the bb-additive convolution. Recall its definition:

(Δb,n​f)​(x)≡(Δb​f)​(x):=f⁡(x)−f⁡(x−b)b(\Delta_{b,n}f)(x)\equiv(\Delta_{b}f)(x):=\frac{f(x)-f(x-b)}{b}

(We use the notation Δb,n\Delta_{b,n} when we want to restrict the domain to ℝn​[x]\mathbb{R}_{n}[x], as in Proposition 3.7 below.) This operator acts on rising factorial polynomials as the usual derivative acts on monomials. That is, for all kk:

Δbx(x+b)⋯(x+(k−1)b)=kx(x+b)⋯(x+(k−2)b)\Delta_{b}x(x+b)\cdots(x+(k-1)b)=kx(x+b)\cdots(x+(k-2)b)

This operator has preservation properties similar to that of the usual derivative and the qq-derivatives. The following result, along with many others regarding mesh and log-mesh polynomials, can be found in [Fis06].

Proposition 3.7.

The operator Δb,n:ℝn​[x]→ℝn−1​[x]\Delta_{b,n}:\mathbb{R}_{n}[x]\to\mathbb{R}_{n-1}[x] preserves the space of bb-mesh polynomials, and the space of strictly bb-mesh polynomials. Further, we have Δb​f≪f\Delta_{b}f\ll f and Δb​f≪f⁡(x−b)\Delta_{b}f\ll f(x-b). If ff is strictly bb-mesh, then these interlacings are strict.

Finding Another Polar Derivative

We now define another “derivative-like” operator that is meant to generalize ∂y\partial_{y} and dq,n∗d_{q,n}^{*}. Notice that unlike Δb\Delta_{b}, this operation depends on nn.

(Δb,n∗​f)​(x):=n​f​(x−b)−(x−b)​Δb​f​(x)(\Delta^{*}_{b,n}f)(x):=nf(x-b)-(x-b)\Delta_{b}f(x)

Unfortunately, this operator does not preserve bb-mesh. However, it does generalize other important properties of ∂y\partial_{y}. In particular, it maps ℝn​[x]\mathbb{R}_{n}[x] to ℝn−1​[x]\mathbb{R}_{n-1}[x], and as b→0b\to 0 it limits to ∂yf\partial_{y}f, the polar derivative of ff with respect to 0. Further, we have the following results.

Lemma 3.8.

Fix f∈ℝn​[x]f\in\mathbb{R}_{n}[x] and write f=∑k=0nakx(x+b)⋯(x+(k−1)b)f=\sum_{k=0}^{n}a_{k}x(x+b)\cdots(x+(k-1)b). Then:

(Δb,n∗f)(x+b)=∑k=0n−1(n−k)akx(x+b)⋯(x+(k−1)b)(\Delta_{b,n}^{*}f)(x+b)=\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}(n-k)a_{k}x(x+b)\cdots(x+(k-1)b)

This next lemma is a generalization of the corollary following it.

Lemma 3.9.

Fix monic polynomials f,g∈ℝ⁡[x]f,g\in\mathbb{R}[x] of degree mm and m−1m-1, respectively, such that gg is strictly bb-mesh and g≪fg\ll f strictly. Denote ha,t​(x):=a​f​(x)−(x−t)​g​(x)h_{a,t}(x):=af(x)-(x-t)g(x) for a≥1a\geq 1 and t>0t>0. For all tt large enough, we have g≪ha,tg\ll h_{a,t} strictly, ha,t≪fh_{a,t}\ll f strictly, and ha,th_{a,t} is strictly bb-mesh.

Proof.

Denote ha,t​(x):=a​f​(x)−(x−t)​g​(x)h_{a,t}(x):=af(x)-(x-t)g(x). Since f,gf,g are monic, we have that ha,th_{a,t} is of degree at most mm with positive leading coefficient (for large tt if a=1a=1). Further, if α1<⋯<αm−1\alpha_{1}<\cdots<\alpha_{m-1} are the roots of gg and β1<⋯<βm\beta_{1}<\cdots<\beta_{m} are the roots of ff, then g≪fg\ll f strictly and tt large implies:

ha,t​(αm−1)=a​f​(αm−1)<0ha,t​(βm)=−(βm−t)​g​(βm)>0ha,t​(αm−2)=a​f​(αm−2)>0ha,t​(βm−1)=−(βm−1−t)​g​(βm−1)<0ha,t​(αm−3)=a​f​(αm−3)<0ha,t​(βm−2)=−(βm−2−t)​g​(βm−2)>0⋮⋮\begin{array}[]{cc}h_{a,t}(\alpha_{m-1})=af(\alpha_{m-1})<0&~~~~~h_{a,t}(\beta_{m})=-(\beta_{m}-t)g(\beta_{m})>0\\ h_{a,t}(\alpha_{m-2})=af(\alpha_{m-2})>0&~~~~~h_{a,t}(\beta_{m-1})=-(\beta_{m-1}-t)g(\beta_{m-1})<0\\ h_{a,t}(\alpha_{m-3})=af(\alpha_{m-3})<0&~~~~~h_{a,t}(\beta_{m-2})=-(\beta_{m-2}-t)g(\beta_{m-2})>0\\ \vdots&~~~~~\vdots\\ \end{array}

The alternating signs imply ha,th_{a,t} has an odd number of roots in the interval (αk,βk+1)(\alpha_{k},\beta_{k+1}) and an even number of roots in the interval (βk,αk)(\beta_{k},\alpha_{k}) for all 1≤k≤m−11\leq k\leq m-1. Since the degree of ha,th_{a,t} is at most mm, each of these intervals must contain exactly one root and zero roots, respectively. If ha,th_{a,t} is of degree mm, then it has one more root which must be real since ha,t∈ℝ⁡[x]h_{a,t}\in\mathbb{R}[x]. Additionally, since ha,th_{a,t} has positive leading coefficient, this last root must lie in the interval (−∞,β1)(-\infty,\beta_{1}) (and not in (βm,∞)(\beta_{m},\infty)). Therefore, g≪ha,tg\ll h_{a,t} strictly and ha,t≪fh_{a,t}\ll f strictly.

Finally, ha,t→gh_{a,t}\to g as t→∞t\to\infty coefficient-wise, and so therefore also in terms of the zeros. This means that the root in the interval (αk,βk+1)(\alpha_{k},\beta_{k+1}) will limit to αk\alpha_{k} from above (for all kk). Further, the possible root in the interval (−∞,β1)(-\infty,\beta_{1}) will then limit to −∞-\infty, as gg is of degree m−1m-1. Since gg is strictly bb-mesh, this implies ha,th_{a,t} is also strictly bb-mesh for large enough tt. ∎

Corollary 3.10.

Let f∈ℝn​[x]f\in\mathbb{R}_{n}[x] be strictly bb-mesh. Then for all t>0t>0 large enough, we have that (t​Δb,n+Δb,n∗)​f(t\Delta_{b,n}+\Delta^{*}_{b,n})f is strictly bb-mesh and Δb,n​f≪(t​Δb,n+Δb,n∗)​f\Delta_{b,n}f\ll(t\Delta_{b,n}+\Delta^{*}_{b,n})f strictly.

Proof.

Consider (t​Δb,n+Δb,n∗)​f=n​f​(x−b)−(x−b−t)​Δb,n​f(t\Delta_{b,n}+\Delta^{*}_{b,n})f=nf(x-b)-(x-b-t)\Delta_{b,n}f. Note that Δb,n​f∈ℝn−1​[x]\Delta_{b,n}f\in\mathbb{R}_{n-1}[x] is strictly bb-mesh and of degree one less than ff, and Δb,n​f≪f⁡(x−b)\Delta_{b,n}f\ll f(x-b) strictly by Proposition 3.7. Now assume WLOG that ff is monic and of degree at least 1. Letting cc denote the leading coefficient of Δb,n​f\Delta_{b,n}f, we have 1≤c≤n1\leq c\leq n. We can then write:

1c​(t​Δb,n+Δb,n∗)​f=nc​f​(x−b)−(x−b−t)​Δb,n​fc\frac{1}{c}(t\Delta_{b,n}+\Delta^{*}_{b,n})f=\frac{n}{c}f(x-b)-(x-b-t)\frac{\Delta_{b,n}f}{c}

Applying the previous lemma to f⁡(x−b)f(x-b) and Δb,n​fc\frac{\Delta_{b,n}f}{c} with a=nca=\frac{n}{c} gives the result. ∎

This corollary says that t​Δb,n+Δb,n∗t\Delta_{b,n}+\Delta^{*}_{b,n} preserves bb-mesh, even though Δb,n∗\Delta_{b,n}^{*} does not. The operator t​Δb,n+Δb,n∗t\Delta_{b,n}+\Delta^{*}_{b,n} can be thought of as the polar derivative with respect to tt, since by limiting b→0b\to 0 we obtain the classical polar derivative.

Recursive Identities

The Δb,n∗\Delta_{b,n}^{*} operator is also required to obtain bb-additive convolution identities similar to Lamprecht’s given above.

Lemma 3.11.

Fix f∈ℝn−1​[x]f\in\mathbb{R}_{n-1}[x] and g∈ℝn​[x]g\in\mathbb{R}_{n}[x]. We have:

f⊞bng=f⊞bn−1Δb,ng(xf)⊞bng=x(f⊞bn−1Δb,ng)+f⊞bn−1Δb,n∗gf\boxplus_{b}^{n}g=f\boxplus_{b}^{n-1}\Delta_{b,n}g~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~(xf)\boxplus_{b}^{n}g=x(f\boxplus_{b}^{n-1}\Delta_{b,n}g)+f\boxplus_{b}^{n-1}\Delta^{*}_{b,n}g
Proof.

The first identity is straightforward from the definition of ⊞bn\boxplus_{b}^{n}. As for the second, we compute:

Δbk​(x​f)=Δbk−1​(x​Δb​f+f⁡(x−b))=⋯=x​Δbk​f+k​Δbk−1​f​(x−b)\Delta_{b}^{k}(xf)=\Delta_{b}^{k-1}(x\Delta_{b}f+f(x-b))=\cdots=x\Delta_{b}^{k}f+k\Delta_{b}^{k-1}f(x-b)

Notice that Δb\Delta_{b} commutes with shifting, so this is unambiguous. This implies:

(xf)⊞bng=∑k=0n(x​Δbk​f+k​Δbk−1​f​(x−b))⋅(Δbn−k​g)​(0)=x(f⊞bn−1Δb,ng)+∑k=1nkΔbk−1f(x−b)⋅(Δbn−kg)(0)=x(f⊞bn−1Δb,ng)+∑k=0n−1Δbn−1−kf(x−b)⋅((n−k)Δbkg)(0)=x(f⊞bn−1Δb,ng)+f(x−b)⊞bn−1(Δb,n∗g)(x+b)\begin{split}(xf)\boxplus_{b}^{n}g&=\sum_{k=0}^{n}(x\Delta_{b}^{k}f+k\Delta_{b}^{k-1}f(x-b))\cdot(\Delta_{b}^{n-k}g)(0)\\ &=x(f\boxplus_{b}^{n-1}\Delta_{b,n}g)+\sum_{k=1}^{n}k\Delta_{b}^{k-1}f(x-b)\cdot(\Delta_{b}^{n-k}g)(0)\\ &=x(f\boxplus_{b}^{n-1}\Delta_{b,n}g)+\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\Delta_{b}^{n-1-k}f(x-b)\cdot((n-k)\Delta_{b}^{k}g)(0)\\ &=x(f\boxplus_{b}^{n-1}\Delta_{b,n}g)+f(x-b)\boxplus_{b}^{n-1}(\Delta_{b,n}^{*}g)(x+b)\end{split}

The last step of the above computation uses Lemma 3.8 and the fact that (Δbk​g)​(0)(\Delta_{b}^{k}g)(0) picks out the coefficient corresponding to the kthk^{\text{th}} rising factorial term. Finally:

f(x−b)⊞bn−1(Δb,n∗g)(x+b)=(f⊞bn−1(Δb,n∗g)(x+b))(x−b)=f⊞bn−1Δb,n∗gf(x-b)\boxplus_{b}^{n-1}(\Delta_{b,n}^{*}g)(x+b)=(f\boxplus_{b}^{n-1}(\Delta_{b,n}^{*}g)(x+b))(x-b)=f\boxplus_{b}^{n-1}\Delta_{b,n}^{*}g

This implies the second identity. ∎

With this we can now emulate Lamprecht’s proof to prove interlacing preserving properties of the bb-additive convolution.

Lamprecht-Style Proof

Theorem 1.8.

Let f,g∈ℝn​[x]f,g\in\mathbb{R}_{n}[x] be strictly bb-mesh polynomials of degree nn. Let Tg:ℝn​[x]→ℝn​[x]T_{g}:\mathbb{R}_{n}[x]\to\mathbb{R}_{n}[x] be the real linear operator defined by Tg:r↦r⊞bngT_{g}:r\mapsto r\boxplus_{b}^{n}g. Then, TgT_{g} preserves interlacing with respect to ff.

Proof.

We prove the theorem by induction. For n=1n=1 the result is straightforward, as ⊞b1≡⊞1\boxplus_{b}^{1}\equiv\boxplus^{1}. For m>1m>1, we inductively assume that the result holds for n=m−1n=m-1. By Corollary 3.5, we only need to show that Tg​[fαk]≪Tg​[f]T_{g}[f_{\alpha_{k}}]\ll T_{g}[f] for all roots αk\alpha_{k} of ff. That is, we want to show fαk⊞bmg≪f⊞bmgf_{\alpha_{k}}\boxplus_{b}^{m}g\ll f\boxplus_{b}^{m}g for all kk.

By Proposition 3.7 and Corollary 3.10, we have that Δb,m​g\Delta_{b,m}g and (t​Δb,m+Δb,m∗)​g(t\Delta_{b,m}+\Delta_{b,m}^{*})g are strictly bb-mesh and Δb,m​g≪(t​Δb,m+Δb,m∗)​g\Delta_{b,m}g\ll(t\Delta_{b,m}+\Delta_{b,m}^{*})g strictly for large enough tt. Further, Δb,m​g\Delta_{b,m}g and (t​Δb,m+Δb,m∗)​g(t\Delta_{b,m}+\Delta_{b,m}^{*})g are of degree m−1m-1. The inductive hypothesis and symmetry of ⊞bn\boxplus_{b}^{n} then imply:

fαk⊞bm−1Δb,mg≪fαk⊞bm−1(tΔb,m+Δb,m∗)gf_{\alpha_{k}}\boxplus_{b}^{m-1}\Delta_{b,m}g\ll f_{\alpha_{k}}\boxplus_{b}^{m-1}(t\Delta_{b,m}+\Delta_{b,m}^{*})g

Considering the discussion near the beginning of the paper, we also have:

fαk⊞bm−1Δb,mg≪(x−αk−t)(fαk⊞bm−1Δb,mg)f_{\alpha_{k}}\boxplus_{b}^{m-1}\Delta_{b,m}g\ll(x-\alpha_{k}-t)(f_{\alpha_{k}}\boxplus_{b}^{m-1}\Delta_{b,m}g)

By properties of ≪\ll, this gives:

fαk⊞bm−1Δb,mg≪(x−αk−t)(fαk⊞bm−1Δb,mg)+fαk⊞bm−1(tΔb,m+Δb,m∗)g=(x−αk)(fαk⊞bm−1Δb,mg)+fαk⊞bm−1Δb,m∗g\begin{split}f_{\alpha_{k}}\boxplus_{b}^{m-1}\Delta_{b,m}g&\ll(x-\alpha_{k}-t)(f_{\alpha_{k}}\boxplus_{b}^{m-1}\Delta_{b,m}g)+f_{\alpha_{k}}\boxplus_{b}^{m-1}(t\Delta_{b,m}+\Delta_{b,m}^{*})g\\ &=(x-\alpha_{k})(f_{\alpha_{k}}\boxplus_{b}^{m-1}\Delta_{b,m}g)+f_{\alpha_{k}}\boxplus_{b}^{m-1}\Delta_{b,m}^{*}g\end{split}

By the above identities and the fact that f⁡(x)=(x−αk)​fαk​(x)f(x)=(x-\alpha_{k})f_{\alpha_{k}}(x), this is equivalent to fαk⊞bmg≪f⊞bmgf_{\alpha_{k}}\boxplus_{b}^{m}g\ll f\boxplus_{b}^{m}g. ∎

Corollary 1.4.

Let f,g∈ℝn​[x]f,g\in\mathbb{R}_{n}[x] be strictly bb-mesh polynomials. Then, f⊞bngf\boxplus_{b}^{n}g is bb-mesh.

Proof.

First suppose f,gf,g are of degree nn. Since f≪f⁡(x−b)f\ll f(x-b) strictly, the previous theorem implies the following:

f⊞bng≪f(x−b)⊞bng=(f⊞bng)(x−b)f\boxplus_{b}^{n}g\ll f(x-b)\boxplus_{b}^{n}g=(f\boxplus_{b}^{n}g)(x-b)

That is, f⊞bngf\boxplus_{b}^{n}g is bb-mesh.

If f,gf,g are not of degree nn, then the result follows by adding new roots and limiting them to ∞\infty, in a fashion similar to the proof of Corollary 1.2 given above. ∎

4 Conclusion

Extensions of other classical convolution results

In this paper we investigate connections between the additive and multiplicative convolutions and their mesh generalizations. Looking forward, it is natural to look at other results in the classical case and ask for mesh generalizations. To the authors knowledge, there are two classical results which have been extended to mesh analogues: in [BKS16], the authors explore extensions of the Hermite-Poulain theorem to the 11-mesh world, and in [Lam16], Lamprecht extends classical results for the multiplicative convolution to the qq-log mesh world.

An important related result in the classical case is the triangle inequality, which we discuss in §2.4. To our knowledge, there is not a known generalization of the triangle inequality to the mesh and log mesh cases. If one could establish such a result for the qq-multiplicative convolution, it would automatically extend to the bb-additive convolution using our analytic connection.

Extensions of other q−q-multiplicative convolution results

In addition to log mesh preservation, Lamprecht proves other results about the qq-multiplicative convolution. Here we comment on these and their relation to the mesh world.

Beyond the finite degree case, Lamprecht discusses the extension of Laguerre-Polya functions to the qq-multiplicative world, and then establishes a qq-version of Polya-Schur multiplier sequences via a power series convolution. Since we are not aware of analogous power series results for the classical additive convolution, we have not explored the connections to the bb-additive case.

Additionally, Lamprecht classifies log-concave sequences in terms of qq-log mesh polynomials using the Hadamard product and a limiting argument. There might be an analogue result in the mesh world for concave sequences, but it is unclear what would take the place of the Hadamard product.

Lamprecht details the classes of polynomials that the qq-multiplicative convolution preserves. Most of these results come from the presence of two poles in the qq-multiplicative case, yielding derivative operators which preserve negative- and positive-rootedness respectively. The bb-additive case does not have such complications. In our simplification of Lamprecht’s argument, we assume the input polynomials to be generic (strictly bb-mesh), and then limit to obtain the result for all bb-mesh polynomials. By keeping track of boundary case information, Lamprecht is able to get more precise results about boundary elements of the space of bb-mesh polynomials. We believe it is likely possible to emulate this in the above proof with more bookkeeping.

The analytic connection applied to other known classical results

There are other results known about the classical multiplicative convolution which we believe could be transferred to the additive convolution using our generic framework. Specifically in [MSS15], Marcus, Spielman, and Srivastava establish a refinement of the triangle inequality for both the additive and multiplicative convolutions. These refinements parallel the well studied transforms from free probability theory. We have not yet worked out the details of this connection.

Further directions for the generic analytic connection

Finally, it is worth nothing that our analytic connection can only transfer results about the multiplicative convolution to the additive convolution. The main obstruction is finding the appropriate analogue to the exponential map. The following limiting connection between exponential polynomials and polynomials motivated our investigation:

limq→11−qx1−q=x\lim_{q\to 1}\frac{1-q^{x}}{1-q}=x

Finding the appropriate “logarithmic analogue” could yield a way to pass results from the additive convolution to the multiplicative convolution. That said, some heuristic evidence suggests that such an analogue might not exist.

Above all, our analytic connection still remains rather mysterious. We suspect that there exists a more general theory which provides better intuition for this multiplicative-to-additive connection. While developing this connection, we found multiple candidate exponential maps which experimentally worked. We settled on the ones introduced in this paper due to their relatively nice combinatorial properties. Ideally, an alternative approach would avoid proving the result on a basis and better explain the role of these “exponential maps”.
